newsitem.title: UK: UK's Labour denies plans to block new gas plants.
newsitem.headline: UK's Labour denies plans to block new gas plants.

text.p: Britain's shadow energy minister John Battle said on Sunday the opposition Labour Party had no plans to block applications to build new gas fired power stations.
He was commenting on an article in the Observer newspaper which said Labour was set to curb the rush by electricity generators to build new gas fired power stations.

"The article in the Observer is incorrect because it creates the impression that Labour will block applications in a blanket fashion when we have no intention of doing that," Battle said in an interview.

Applicants are assessed on a case by case basis and it will remain so under Labour, he said. "But inevitably there will be growing objections from local people to planning as we get more applications."
Electricity and oil companies that want to build gas fired power stations have to apply to the Trade and Industry Secretary for consent.
Since 1990 consent has been granted for 27 gas fired plants and applications for more than 20 have been submitted.
There are fears that Britain's growing dependency on gas will mean it has to rely increasingly on imported supplies.
Labour party policy is "to make sense of securing diverse, secure and sustainable supplies of energy," Battle said.
"And that means we have to take some responsibility for ensuring that we are not totally dependent on importing gas as our only source of fuel in the early decades of the next century."
The proportion of Britain's electricity generated by gas is predicted to rise to more than 60 percent by 2010, unless there is a change in government policy.
In 1990 the figure was less than one percent, 70 percent of the UK's electricity came from coal fired stations.
